newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel denies politics tied to rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel denies politics tied to rate cut.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel on Sunday denied political considerations influenced his decision to lower interest rates sharply after the cabinet approved changes in the exchange rate regime.

"There had been a long period of uncertainty, which created a lot of sensitivity in the money and capital markets. It was very important to end it," Frenkel said, explaining his surprise decision to cut the central bank's key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points last Wednesday to 12.7 percent.

He said the central bank's only considerations were falling inflation and inflationary expectations and the slowing economy. He also cited the measures taken by the cabinet at an emergency meeting on Wednesday to ease foreign currency controls and adjust the exchange rate system.
"The decision was made only with these factors taken into account -- period," Frenkel said.
Frenkel's remarks come amid charges that he had a hand in bringing about Finance Minister Dan Meridor's abrupt resignation last Wednesday.

Meridor, a political rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has charged that the timing and method Netanyahu used to bring the decision to the cabinet was meant to embarrass him, leaving him no choice but to resign.
Meridor has not specifically charged Frenkel with involvement, but media commentators have suggested the governor aided Netanyahu.

In a commentary on Sunday, the daily newspaper Maariv recalled that Frenkel had been a candidate for finance minister in the Netanyahu government and was supposed to head a planned council of economic advisers.

"We expected to continue seeing close cooperation between the prime minister's and the governor's office....That reached a peak in the 'Diagonol Affair,' in which the governor joined with the prime minister in helping him to indirectly force out the finance minister," the newspaper said.

The Bank of Israel was originally due to make its monthly interest rate announcement this Monday, at which time economists had expected only a mild cut of about 0.5 percentage point. Interest rates had been unchanged since the end of February.

Early last week, however, speculation the central bank would succeed in its long-running campaign to widen the diagonal currency band created huge speculative pressure on the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to intervene heavily.

Since the start of the year, the shekel has pressed the lower limit of its trading band against the basket of foreign currencies to which it is pegged. The market assumed that if the band was widened the shekel would be free to appreciate.

The exchange rate adjustments approved by the cabinet did not affect the lower end of the band but reduced the incline of the slope, enabling the currency to strengthen more than it would have under the previous system.

In Friday trading, the dollar unexpectedly gained ground on the shekel, with the representative rate set at 3.437 shekels, up 0.53 percent from Thursday. The currency basket also strengthened against the shekel, rising 0.57 percent to 3.7343.
There is no foreign currency trading in Israel on Sunday.
